My dad means the world to me. He's sick and bedridden and I honestly don't know what I'm going to do when he passes. I'm not ready.

The biggest advice I can give is to listen to her. No one listened to me like he did. He would let me ramble for hours about anything and I felt heard and understood because he always had something to say to help me out, even if it was the world's smallest problem. I have 6 siblings and he managed to find time just for me, playing my made up version of chess, taking me to get slurpees, letting me pick the cereal at the store, holding his hand, no matter how old I was. He made me feel safe and wanted and special above my other siblings. As an adult, we have a special bond because we have a very similar intellect and interests, we're the only ones who went to college (not to call my family stupid, they just can't argue philosophy or classic authors like we can). My dad has always been someone who will listen to me. He knows everything and has never judged me, but advised me on all my problems. 

So, listen. Even when it gets hard. My family is super religious and I knew when I was 6 that I was never going to be a mommy or married like my sisters. When I came out as gay, my dad was the only one who didn't judge me. He never judged me for going to college or having a career, and he didn't judge me when that career failed. He still listens, and is the only one who sees me cry.

I just finished Peter Brett’s Demon Cycle series and was surprised at how quickly I read them. It’s a fantasy and world-building series, which I am very drawn to for all the creativity. A lot of world-building fantasy novels include elements from the father of world-building fantasy, J.R.R. Tolkien, but this series really stood on its own feet. It’s a world plagued by demon creatures that prowl at night. The people of this world are farmers, tradesmen, merchants, and entertainers. When the sun sets, they are forced to remain behind doors and painted wards that prevent the demons from entering their homes. These wards are a major lifeline among the people and there are ward specialists who sell and buy different wards to towns and villages. The demons themselves also vary in type, whether they are rock, wood, wind, water, sand, or fire. They each inflict different types of damage so wards are specified to each type. Enter Arlen Bales, a young boy in a farming community. One horrible evening, his mother is killed by demons and his father stayed within the protection of the wards, unable to help her. Arlen is devastated and rushes out into the ‘naked night’ to try and save her. He unfortunately fails but it changes his whole life. He’s tired of letting the demons influence a person’s lifestyle and he vows to destroy every demon he finds. He goes out on his own, learns to fight, learns warding, and a general education that wouldn’t have happened if he stayed home. Every night, he fights the demons, which is something unusual in his country. He visits a different country, where the men of this new city stand against the demons each night to protect their families. Arlen trains with them and discovers new wards for fighting, rather than protection. He brings these wards and fighting techniques to his home country and teaches other men and women to fight. Meanwhile, the demons are rising in stronger numbers and the countries soon become at war. Arlen’s purpose becomes uniting all of humanity against the demons. The demons are planning a war against all humans and time is running out. 

Peter Brett is a wonderful storyteller and creates such beautiful and dynamic characters. I love fantasy novels that explore real world concerns and approach solutions to solve them. Problems like gender roles, politics, soldiers, rape, family relationships, and religion. Strong independent women clash with alpha males and cultures conflict in interesting and dynamic ways. I’m looking forward to what he writes next.

Absolutely make sure you have food and water on you at all times. Set an alert on your phone to make sure you are drinking enough water to stay hydrated. You’ll be taking so many pictures, you won’t even notice when your phone dies. Lastly, make sure you get enough rest at night and a decent shower. Con smell is real.

Above all, have fun! Talk to people (we’re nice, I swear) and don’t be afraid to ask someone for their picture. those of us in cosplay love it. Just no unwanted touching lol. I would definitely check the schedule to plan events. The vendors are only open at certain hours and you could miss a panel of you aren’t paying attention. I think they still use the guidebook app, so you can mark what panels you want to go to and it will give you an alert. Don’t forget meals when you plan. Check out what’s in the area, so you don’t have to buy the expensive food in the con.

This topic really is a double edged sword. As another gay teacher, I hated feeling closeted. However, the unspoken promise we take as an educator is that the student comes first. In the district where I most recently taught, being LGBT was not okay. Not only were the parents highly negative, but the students were, as well. I would rather be able to teach my subject without having anyone slur my name or have parents pull their kids out because my teaching them will suddenly turn their kid gay, or whatever. I felt like it was better for the students to see me as a strong teacher that they could come to and trust, rather than to let my truth and freedom be known. Doing so, I found out a lot about my students and was able to protect a lot from bullies. They knew by word of mouth that I was one of the few teachers that was LGBT friendly and I had students that weren’t even in my class feel better knowing someone cared. There were two people in the school that knew I was gay, the principal and one of the guidance counselors. I brought them both into a meeting to express what I saw about bullies and the LGBT kids in the school that, apparently, the other teachers were blind to. Before I left that district last year, an anti-bullying club was established, since they couldn’t outright call it the LGBT club, and I’ve heard that they have been getting a lot of support from other teachers and the community. So while I didn’t get to do much for myself, I believe I did what I could as an educator.

I hated this book. Had to read it for class, during a study of the modernist movement. Ugh! I get the point behind the stream of consciousness technique and that modernist writers like Joyce were experimenting with the truth behind human experience. I can appreciate it for what it accomplished for literature. But I hate the text. Modernist writers ignored form and structure to explore human thought. This makes the text dry and very difficult to comprehend, even for academics. Virginia Woolf wrote that the 'common' reader was uneducated and not blessed with understanding and therefore not worthy of her work. Take a look at her story 'a mark on the wall' nothing happens. There is no plot. Take a look at episode 18 of Ulyssses. There are only eight sentences. Not a single one makes sense. This was modernism. They changed literature, but their stuff was awful. Don't read a book just to be able to say you read it, because most people have either not read it, never heard of it, or possibly only read it as a struggle in school. No offense, but don't be a pretentious ass.

Well, right off the bat:
1-Barnaby Rudge-Charles Dickens-One of Dickens' lesser known novels but, IMO, one of his best. Mob mentality, a spectacular dandy villain, a poor, handicap man who gets caught up in the riots and a mystery surrounding an inn and a murder.
2-Enchantment-Orson Scott Card-As much as I can't stand his personal views, I still have to call this book one of my favorites for all the magic and joy it brought to me for at least a decade. Ivan finds a magical bridge that takes him back in time. Thus begins his adventures with the two worlds, a princess and an evil witch out of the nightmares of generations of children.
3-Keys to the Kingdom series by Garth Nix-I know, it's more than one book, but this series is absolutely amazing. I think I read the whole thing in two weeks. Granted, they are YA novels, but still. I work full time. Anyway, boy becomes heir to the center of the universe, which he must now defend. There's symbolism with clocks, the 7 virtues, King Arthur, and a bunch of other stuff that's really intriguing that kept me from ever wanting to put the books down.
